960.dq: Typologically this has to be classified as a tone, for such a stress may be entirely absent from non-clitic words, e.g. bəta 'dust' vs. bətá 'louse', respectively interpretable as Mid-Mid Mid-High.
960.dloc: Hetzron 1976, fascicle p. 12 (= AAL 3, 42), section 4.1.3 'Prosody' (archive.org page n13); Appleyard 2007 p. 482 fn. 4; Fallon 2001 p. 50
960.prule: No positional stress rule is stated by any reachable source. Hetzron 1976 classifies Bilin typologically as a (non-musical) tone language: the 'stressed' syllable carries high pitch, often spreading to following syllables; this prominence is not obligatory ('may be entirely absent from non-clitic words') and its presence is lexically contrastive (bəta 'dust' Mid-Mid vs. bətá 'louse' Mid-High). Appleyard 2007 fn. 4 (reporting Palmer 1957/1958): 'varying prominence patterns, i.e., varying patterns of accent placement' that contribute to the paradigms and occasionally distinguish otherwise identical verbal forms; placement varies between Reinisch, Palmer and Appleyard's own data and is affected by sentence rhythm, so stress-accent is left unmarked. Fallon 2001 p. 50 sets 'tonal or pitch accent phenomena' aside. Wikipedia (carrying Fallon 2004, unreachable): possible pitch accent, prominent syllable always high-toned, not every word has one.
960.quote: Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress. Inadequate work on the other Agaw tongues makes it impossible to make any statement about tone elsewhere. 960.tone: Hetzron 1976 p. 12: 'Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress.... In Bilin, tone is not truly musical. The stressed syllable has high pitch which is "often carried through to following syllables" (Tucker-Bryan 1966:500, after Palmer). Typologically this has to be classified as a tone, for such a stress may be entirely absent from non-clitic words' -- i.e. a culminative, non-obligatory, lexically contrastive high-pitch accent (pitch-accent/restricted tone), analysed by Hetzron as Mid vs High tone. Fallon 2001 p. 50: 'Tonal or pitch accent phenomena have posed problems for many investigators and will not be described here.' Wikipedia (carrying Fallon 2004, not reachable): 'It may have pitch accent (Fallon 2004) as prominent syllables always have a high tone, but not all words have such a syllable.' Appleyard 2007 uses the label 'stress-accent' but marks nothing and reports inter-source variation in placement. No source states a stress rule; the accent's placement/presence is lexical-paradigmatic.

morph.rootq: "In words of over three syllables stress placement depends upon the morphological composition of the word. In words with two free morphemes such as [xùwikapέtεw] 'my ribs' each morpheme (/xui/, /kapete/) is stressed on the penult. In monomorphemic words exceeding three syllables, which are quite rare, primary stress appears to be penultimate, with secondary stress on alternating syllables to the left" (§2.2, p.99). The statement refers to free morphemes/morphological composition, not to root vs. affix as such; the only affixes in the stressed examples are non-syllabic possessor suffixes ([nímεw] 'my hand', [xùwikapέtεw] 'my ribs').

967.prule: No established word-stress rule. 970.tone: Woodward 1882 says nothing about tone. Modern primary evidence (reached in Stage B, re-read in Stage C): Cassimjee & Kisseberth ROA-176, from their own consultants (p.21 fn.5: 'This discussion of Kibondei is based on fairly extensive data that we have collected from Josephine Yambi and her uncle, David Kishe'), treat Kibondei as a privative-H tone language: p.21 'In Kibondei, there is clear evidence that if there is just one sponsor of High tone in the word, the domain initiated by that sponsor will extend as far as the penult syllable of the word', with toneless vs H contrasts (18) n[i]-a-senga 'I am cutting' vs [a]-a-sénga '(s)he is cutting', H stems (19) n[i]-a-bundúga 'I am pounding'; the domain is word-bounded (23: 'asénga nyama... *asenga nyáma'); p.39 'Kibondei is a shifting language, therefore the High tone is heard only on the penult vowel of the word'; p.42 'In Kibondei, an IP-final High tone is not pronounced'. C&K make no statement about stress/accent in Kibondei. Consequence: in the general case a word containing an H realises it on the word penult, exactly where Woodward hears 'accent', so the 1882 penult accent is confounded with surface H placement (toneless words such as niasenga carry no H at all; a stem-final H can cross onto a following word, n[i]-a-da nyáma). Penult prominence coexisting with H attraction to the penult is the standard Seuta analysis (cf. Zigula, Shambaa), so the two sources are not irreconcilable and no reachable source denies word…

tn.quote: 1. There are two tones, high (H) and low (L). The marked tone is low. The general default tone is high (although the default for final syllables is low). … Bora has two contrastive level tones. It has no contour tones. There are—to our knowledge—no restrictions between tones and segments: either tone may occur on any syllable. Every syllable carries either a high or low tone. High tones may occur one after the other without limit … The tone bearing unit (tbu) is the syllable, not the mora. The basic tone-assignment rules are blind to vowel length; they deal with syllables, not moras

977.prule: Accent (intensity + length, carrying the H vs HL tone contrast) falls invariably on the final (or only) syllable of each morpheme; it is demarcative of morpheme boundaries (prefixes excepted: they integrate into the base). In polymorphemic words, often only one morpheme-final syllable keeps full intensity and distinctive tone (primary), the other morpheme-final syllables keep length/timbre as secondary accents; in compounds/reduplications the word-final accented syllable is always realized weak and low, so primary is non-final. Word-level position therefore follows morphological composition, not syllable count.
977.srule: In polymorphemic words the final syllable of every non-prefix morpheme other than the one carrying the main accent bears a secondary accent: it loses the extra intensity and its H/HL tone is neutralized to mid or low, but it keeps relative vowel length and full vowel quality and blocks nasal spreading ('Ces syllabes peuvent ainsi être considérées comme portant un accent secondaire'). Placement follows morpheme boundaries, not syllable count.

evidence_works.detail: Abstract-only evidence. What the abstract reports measuring: the starting and end points of the Bribri tones on a five-level pitch scale, compared statistically: high and falling tones share a starting point (p(1,118)=1.9, p=0.17) and both differ from the low tone's starting point; the end points of the three tones differ (p(2,136)=40.0, p<0.00001), giving high [45], falling [43], low [11]; the rising tone starts like the low tone but ends higher, [13] (p(1,5)=7.1, p<0.05; both rising-tone tests have df (1,5)). Syllables with codas attract contour tones (F(3,859)=17.6, p<0.0001); [+high] register tones are 'associated with voiceless onsets and high vowels' (no statistic given in the abstract). Finding relevant to the entry: syllables 'supposed to be "neutral"' are [3] before a [+high]-register tone (high, falling) and [1] before a [-high] tone (low, rising), 'suggesting a register spread from the final toned syllable to those preceding it'. The abstract does not say which of Chevrier's classes its 'neutral' syllables correspond to (unaccented syllables, 'produites avec un ton bas par défaut', or non-primary morpheme-final syllables whose tone is 'neutralisé à moyen ou bas'); in either case it adds a conditioning factor (the register of the following toned syllable) that the record does not state. It does not bear on stress placement.

981.prule: Free (lexical, phonemic) word stress: position not predictable, may fall on any syllable (initial, final, or medial); minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone; stress shifts within inflectional/derivational paradigms (e.g. masc./neut. nouns sg. vs pl., fem. zero-ending nouns in the definite, some aorists).
981.srule: None in non-compound words: one stress per word even at 6-7 syllables, no rhythmic/alternating secondary stresses ('These words haven't secondary stress... A secondary stress occurs only in some complex words in slow speech rate'); in some compounds, in slow speech, a secondary stress sits on the first member's own lexically stressed syllable, 0-4 syllables from the main stress (e.g. stógodíšnina, tjutjúnoproizvódstvo). Not mentioned in Leafgren 2011 (Ch. 2 'Stress Alternation', pp. 19-21).

tn.quote: Фонологичната интонационна система на съвременния български книжовен език се състои от пет интонационни акцента (L*, L*+H, L+H*, H*, H+!H*), три фразови акцента (L-, Н-, !H-) и четири гранични тона (%H, L%, H%, !H%). Високият таргет в интонационните акценти, фразовите акценти и граничните тонове може да бъде модифициран чрез понижаване (downstep) или повишаване (upstep) спрямо предходния висок таргет. … [с. 39] При реализацията на акцентите често се наблюдава нестабилно синхронизиране на тоналния таргет с границите на лексикално ударената сричка.
tn.translation: The phonological intonation system of Contemporary Standard Bulgarian consists of five pitch accents (L*, L*+H, L+H*, H*, H+!H*), three phrase accents (L-, H-, !H-) and four boundary tones (%H, L%, H%, !H%). The high target in the pitch accents, phrase accents and boundary tones can be modified by lowering (downstep) or raising (upstep) relative to the preceding high target. ... [p. 39] In the realization of the accents, unstable alignment of the tonal target with the boundaries of the lexically stressed syllable is often observed.

tn.locator: p. 44, section 3 'Интонационна фонология на българския език' + abstract p. 39
tn.note: No lexical tone: pitch is intonational only. Five post-lexical pitch accents dock on the lexically stressed syllable, with three phrase accents and four boundary tones (downstepped !H variants).

985.tone: Margery Peña 1982 (Ujarrás idiolect, informant Esteban Beita Ríos): two tonemes, high (marked acute) and low, with tonal minimal pairs; low tone has a falling allotone on final syllable nuclei and monosyllabic morphemes; high tone has a rising allotone conditioned by utterance phonology. No word-stress rule; instead a weak/strong syllable partition inside the word computed from tone position (strong = first high-toned syllable onward, or only the final syllable if no high tone); strong-syllable vowels are perceived as long. Bourland Hawley 1975 (also an Ujarrás-born informant, José Raúl Villanueva Vargas; Margery's note 2 labels the study '[de Ujarrás]') explicitly denies tone ('no es una lengua de tonos') and posits three phonemic accent levels (débil/primario/intenso) proved by minimal pairs, rejecting Pozas 1944's two-tone analysis; the disagreement is analytical, not dialectal. Later scholarship (Margery 1989 dictionary; González Campos & Lehmann: 'the acute marks high tone') sides with the tonal analysis.

tn.quote: 3. Tonemas. De acuerdo con una hipótesis de Constenla (comunicación personal) el idiolecto examinado mostró en el nivel fonemático la existencia de dos tonos: alto y bajo. El tono bajo (no representado en la transcripción fonológica) detenta un alotono descendente ([ ^]) cuya aparición se da contreñida a núcleos silábicos en posición final así como a núcleos de morfemas monosilábicos. Por su parte el tono alto (/ ´/) presenta un alotono ascendente … Algunos ejemplos de contrastes tonales son los siguientes: … / ua / [u̯a] 'con (instrumental)', / uá / 'zorro hediondo' …
tn.translation: 3. Tonemes. According to a hypothesis of Constenla (personal communication) the idiolect examined showed at the phonemic level the existence of two tones: high and low. The low tone (not represented in the phonological transcription) has a falling allotone ([ ^]) whose appearance is restricted to syllable nuclei in final position as well as to nuclei of monosyllabic morphemes. For its part the high tone (/´/) presents a rising allotone … Some examples of tonal contrasts are the following: … /ua/ 'with (instrumental)', /uá/ 'skunk' …
tn.cite: Margery Peña, Enrique. 1982. Descripción del sistema fonológico de un idiolecto del cabécar de Ujarrás. Estudios de Lingüística Chibcha 1: 33-44.
tn.note: Two level tones, high (acute) and low, with minimal pairs; falling and rising pitches are allotones; strong vs weak syllables follow from tone. Bourland 1975 instead posits three accent levels.
